meta.title: Climate
meta.intro: Climate controls, monsoon mechanism, India’s seasons, rainfall distribution and regional climatic variation.

Connect physical geography with people, resources, environment and development.

blocks.text: Weather is the state of the atmosphere over a place at a particular time. Climate is the sum total of weather conditions and variations over a large area for a long period, generally more than thirty years.
The elements of weather and climate are temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity and precipitation. Weather may change within hours, while climate describes long-term patterns and averages.
India has a monsoon-type climate. Despite an overall seasonal rhythm, temperature and rainfall differ widely because of latitude, altitude, relief, distance from the sea and atmospheric circulation.
Latitude affects the angle and intensity of solar energy. The Tropic of Cancer passes through India, giving the country both tropical and subtropical climatic characteristics.
Altitude generally reduces temperature with increasing height. The Himalayas also protect much of the subcontinent from extremely cold winds from Central Asia.
Pressure and wind systems move heat and moisture. Distance from the sea moderates temperatures in coastal areas, while inland areas often experience greater seasonal extremes.
Relief influences rainfall. Mountains force moisture-bearing winds to rise, causing rain on windward slopes and drier conditions on leeward slopes. The Western Ghats are an important example.
The word monsoon comes from the Arabic mausim, meaning season. It refers to the seasonal reversal in the direction of prevailing winds during the year.

During summer, intense heating creates low pressure over northwestern India and adjoining parts of Asia. The Indian Ocean remains relatively higher in pressure, encouraging moisture-bearing winds to move towards the land.
Southeast trade winds cross the Equator and are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. They reach India as the southwest monsoon and split into the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches.

The Arabian Sea branch brings heavy rain to the windward Western Ghats and advances towards northwestern India. The Bay of Bengal branch moves towards northeast India and then westward along the Ganga plains.
The monsoon has active and break periods. Depressions, local relief and changing atmospheric circulation influence the timing and amount of rainfall.

The cold weather season generally lasts from mid-November to February in northern India. Northeast trade winds prevail. Western disturbances bring winter rain to northwestern plains and snowfall in the Himalayas.

The hot weather season broadly extends from March to May. Temperatures rise, low pressure develops over northwestern India, and hot dry winds called loo affect parts of the north. Local thunderstorms and pre-monsoon showers occur in some regions.

The advancing southwest monsoon is the main rainy season, broadly from June to September. It generally reaches the Kerala coast first and advances across the country. Much of India receives a major share of annual rainfall during this period.

The retreating monsoon occurs mainly in October and November. Winds withdraw from northwestern India. Low-pressure systems and cyclones over the Bay of Bengal may bring rain to the eastern coast, especially Tamil Nadu.
Rainfall is unevenly distributed. The windward Western Ghats and parts of northeastern India receive very heavy rainfall, while western Rajasthan, Ladakh and rain-shadow areas receive much less.

The Bay of Bengal branch generally loses moisture as it moves westward across the Northern Plains, so rainfall tends to decrease towards the west. Coastal areas usually have a smaller annual temperature range than inland areas.
Climate influences crops, water availability, housing, clothing, health, transport and livelihoods. Droughts, floods, heat waves, cold waves and cyclones can cause serious human and economic losses.
Map practice: mark the Western Ghats, Meghalaya plateau, Thar Desert, Ladakh, Tamil Nadu coast and the broad direction of both southwest monsoon branches.
